subject: Medicine
summary: Vasculitis is inflammation of vessel walls that can cause ischemia and organ damage. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues, imaging, and biopsy, with treatment targeting the underlying cause and inflammation.

sections.p: Vasculitis refers to immune‑mediated inflammation of arteries, veins or capillaries, leading to vessel wall damage and tissue ischemia. Diagnosis combines clinical features, laboratory markers, imaging, and often a tissue biopsy.
b: Clinical suspicion based on systemic or organ‑specific signs

t.b: Detects autoantibodies against neutrophil antigens; positive suggests ANCA‑associated vasculitis (e.g., GPA, MPA).
Confirms pauci‑immune necrotizing glomerulonephritis; guides severity and treatment.

sections.p: Severity is staged by organ involvement and damage. The Five‑Factor Score (FFS) or BVAS score guides prognosis and treatment intensity.
b: Mild: isolated skin or ENT disease

sections.p: Primary causes are autoimmune; secondary causes include infections, drugs, and systemic diseases common in low‑resource settings.
Presentation varies with vessel size and organ. Common features include fever, weight loss, skin lesions, arthralgia, and organ‑specific signs such as hematuria or cough.
Investigations aim to confirm vasculitis type, assess severity, and rule out mimics.

sections.p: Urgent complications include rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, pulmonary hemorrhage, and aneurysm rupture.
Treat the underlying cause, control inflammation, and support organ function. First‑line agents are steroids and immunosuppressants; biologics are added if refractory.

t.b: Induction in severe disease; chosen for rapid immunosuppression but avoided in pregnancy due to teratogenicity.
Maintenance therapy; preferred over methotrexate in renal disease.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of disease activity, organ function, and drug toxicity is essential. Vaccination and infection control reduce secondary triggers.
Conditions that mimic vasculitis include infections, connective tissue diseases, and drug reactions.
Some tests may be falsely normal early or due to concurrent infections. Clinical correlation is mandatory.

faq.q: What is the most common type of vasculitis?
faq.a: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener) is common in adults, especially with ENT and lung involvement.
